newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wage rise benign for inflation, rates.
newsitem.headline: Australian wage rise benign for inflation, rates.

text.p: Low paid Australian workers were granted a A$10 (US$7.70) a week pay rise on Tuesday by the Australian Industrial Relations Commission -- but the rise fell short of the A$20 sought by unions in their "living wage" case.
The Commission, Australia's industrial relations tribunal, also set a A$359.40 per week minimum wage, which was below the union claim for A$380 a week minimum wage.
The Commission said the union claims would have increased average wage inflation to six percent per year and forced the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to raise interest rates.
The A$10 pay rise is for workers who have failed to negotiate a wage rise through direct bargaining with employers.
Economists welcomed the wage rise, saying it did not endanger Australia's low inflation rate or threaten to push up interest rates.
"I think basically low inflation for the next year or so is now locked in," said Michael Blythe, senior economist with the Commonwealth Bank.
The government's Bureau of Statistics will unveil Australia's latest inflation figures on Wednesday, for the period ended March 31.
Market economists are tipping 2.1 percent underlying inflation for the year to March, comfortably within the RBA's target range of two to three percent.
Richard Yetsenga, economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said: "I don't think there really are any rates implications from it". Official cash interest rates are currently 6.0 percent.
